analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the Treasury's federal insurance oversight office and replaces it with a narrower international insurance office.
analysis.headline: The bill to eliminate the Federal Insurance Office, introduced January 16, 2026 with 5 Republican cosponsors and no Democratic support, was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and has had no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill shuts down the Federal Insurance Office, the Treasury branch created by the 2010 Dodd-Frank law to monitor the insurance industry, and replaces it with a smaller "United States Insurance Representative" focused on international insurance negotiations and the federal terrorism insurance program. It keeps a Treasury appointee's power to override state insurance rules only in narrow cases involving foreign insurers, and it explicitly preserves state rules on rates, coverage, antitrust, and solvency. It also adds one state insurance commissioner to the Financial Stability Oversight Council, appointed by the President.
analysis.who_benefits: The insurance industry gains the most: the federal office that monitors its markets is eliminated and replaced with a much narrower office focused on international prudential matters. State insurance regulators also gain a seat at the Financial Stability Oversight Council. For ordinary insurance consumers, the practical change is small, since the eliminated office monitored and reported but did not directly regulate rates or coverage.

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates the Federal Insurance Office and the Director position, shrinking the federal footprint over an industry that is otherwise regulated by the states.

Preserves the industry's preferred regulatory structure: the bill expressly does not preempt state rules on rates, premiums, underwriting, sales practices, coverage requirements, capital and solvency, or the application of state antitrust laws to insurance.

Gives the insurance industry a voice in systemic-risk oversight by adding a state insurance commissioner to the Financial Stability Oversight Council, the panel that watches for threats to the financial system.

analysis.who_pays: Direct costs are minimal — the new office uses existing Treasury staff and resources. The indirect cost falls on insurance consumers and the public, who lose the only federal office that monitors insurance markets and reports on industry conditions, leaving fewer eyes on an industry that sells nearly every household a policy.

drawbacks.text: Eliminating the Federal Insurance Office removes the federal government's dedicated window into the insurance industry, including its data-gathering and reporting on market conditions, leaving federal policymakers and the public with less visibility into risks that build up across state lines.

The bill hands a Treasury appointee the power to preempt state insurance measures when they treat foreign insurers less favorably and conflict with a negotiated international agreement — a power exercised with notice, comment, and a 30-day waiting period, but still an override of state law decided inside one executive agency.

Making the Financial Stability Oversight Council's insurance seat a presidential appointment, with only a nonbinding recommendation list from state regulators, politicizes a position currently held by an independent state official.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a modest reorganization with real but limited stakes. Its consumer-facing safeguards are genuine — state rate regulation, antitrust, and solvency rules are untouched, and the preemption power is narrower than the office it replaces in some respects. But the bill's main effect is to shrink federal scrutiny of the insurance industry, and its benefits flow mostly to insurers who prefer state-based regulation and less federal monitoring. The public loses a federal monitoring capability and gains little in return, so on balance the trade favors the industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a vote, or any further action.

narrative.text: Representative Troy Downing introduced the bill on January 16, 2026, joined by Representatives Fitzgerald and Ogles as original cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, and the record shows no further action — no committee markup, no floor vote, no movement since.
Five Republicans have cosponsored the bill; no Democrat has.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has come out ahead yet. The bill is sitting in committee, and the Federal Insurance Office it targets still exists, so the current state of affairs is unchanged from before the bill was filed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — bill is dormant in committee

sides.party_line_note: There have been no votes, so no partisan split is on the record; all five cosponsors are Republicans out of 223 House Republicans, with no Democratic support listed.

industries.note: The bill eliminates the federal office that monitors the industry's markets and replaces it with a much smaller international-focused office, leaving insurers under state regulation with less federal scrutiny. State rules on rates, coverage, antitrust, and solvency are explicitly preserved, so the immediate change is the loss of a federal watchdog rather than any new burden on consumers.

The bill carries over a preemption process under which state measures can be overridden only if they discriminate against foreign reinsurers and conflict with a U.S. international agreement — no broader opening of state markets.

Regulators lose a formal federal counterpart office that consulted with them, but gain a dedicated state insurance commissioner seat on the Financial Stability Oversight Council, appointed by the President from a state-regulator-recommended list.

analysis.trajectory: Most bills introduced in the House die in committee without a hearing or vote, and this one shows the usual signs: a single committee referral, five cosponsors, and no action more than a month in. Unless the Financial Services Committee schedules it, it will likely lapse when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027.
